shoulder-width-training-lateral-raises-d.text: Users train the side delts, mostly with lateral raises, to make the shoulders look wider and improve frame proportions. Forum members post bideltoid measurements and compare them against height. Muscle growth is well established; its effect on rated attractiveness is based on anecdote.

v-taper-shoulder-to-waist-ratio.text: Lifters and looksmaxxers aim for a shoulder-to-waist ratio near 1.6 by building the shoulders and back while cutting waist fat. The ratio is a bodybuilding ideal, and the 1.6 target is forum-quoted rather than drawn from a specific attractiveness study.

biacromial-clavicle-width.text: Looksmaxxers treat biacromial and clavicle width as the fixed skeletal base that muscle can add to but not change. Specific bideltoid numbers are quoted as marks of a high-status frame, a belief from forum discussion rather than studied thresholds.

clavicle-lengthening-osteotomy.text: Discussed in hardmaxxing circles as an extreme surgery to widen the shoulders by lengthening the collarbones. It is raised as a rare option and is not an established cosmetic operation; no cosmetic studies were found.

stomach-vacuum-waist-training.text: Users practice the stomach vacuum to train the transversus abdominis and make the waist look smaller, supporting a V-taper. The muscle is well described anatomically; its use for waist appearance is based on anecdote with little research.

neckmaxxing-neck-training.text: Neckmaxxers train the neck to make it thicker, believing this adds a masculine, dominant look and better face and frame proportions. Neck-to-jaw ratio targets circulate on forums, and no published study validates them.

grip-and-forearm-training.text: Lifters use wrist curls, hangs, carries and grippers to build forearm size and grip strength, valued for the look of the arms. Strength gains are well documented in sport; the claim that thick forearms look more attractive is anecdotal.

calisthenics-gymnast-physique.text: People use push-ups, pull-ups, dips and skills like levers to build a lean, muscular, gymnast-style body with little equipment. Bodyweight training is studied for strength and muscle; its aesthetic results specifically have limited direct evidence.

ring-training-planche-progressions.text: Practitioners use ring dips, levers and planche progressions as a skill-based route to upper-body size and a gymnast look. The gymnast build is the draw; no studies on appearance outcomes were found.

chain: More size, then cut to reveal it
dirty-bulk-lean-bulk.text: Lifters eat in a surplus to gain muscle, either a large loosely tracked one (dirty bulk) or a small controlled one (lean bulk), usually followed by a cut. Bulking and cutting come from bodybuilding practice; the relative merits of each style are debated by forum posters.

anabolic-diet-high-calorie-eating.text: The 1990s Anabolic Diet is a cyclic ketogenic bodybuilding plan, grouped with heavy-eating approaches to gaining size. It is promoted for building muscle, and no studies of its appearance results were found.

beef-organ-liver-diet.text: Followers eat beef liver and other organ meats as a dense source of vitamins and minerals, a trend spread partly by fitness influencers. Users link this to better training and general condition; its use for appearance is anecdotal.

deltoid-shoulder-implants.text: Discussed in hardmaxxing circles as a surgical way to add width and roundness to the shoulders for a V-shaped upper body. The contour change would be visible directly; research found is on joint replacement, not cosmetic use.

padded-shoulders-structured-jackets.text: Padded shoulders and structured jackets add visible width and a more athletic silhouette immediately, with no training or surgery. Users also say pads visually straighten sloping clavicles. The look is backed by fashion history rather than attractiveness studies.

horizontal-stripes-and-layering-for-widt.text: People wear horizontal stripes and layers to look broader across the chest and shoulders; layers add real volume and stripes are said to draw the eye sideways. The visual effect is immediate, and no direct studies were found.

gymnastic-rings.text: Suspended rings are used for bodyweight training, with the gymnast physique as the draw. Men's still rings is a strength-heavy gymnastics event. No studies compare rings for looks.

fat-gripz-grip-thickeners.text: Users attach thick rubber sleeves to bars and dumbbells to challenge grip and forearms for arm size. One acute study exists, and none examine forearm size or appearance.

ems-suit-electrical-muscle-stimulation.text: Whole-body EMS suits are sold for fitness and toning on the idea that stimulated contractions build muscle. EMS is established in rehab and small fitness trials exist; its effect on looks is untested.

gynecomastia-surgery.text: Men use male breast reduction to remove glandular tissue and fat for a flatter chest, which suits shirtless and fitted-clothing looks. The change is visible directly. It is the established medical route when enlargement persists.

chin-tucks.text: Users do chin tucks to improve head posture and, in some accounts, to sharpen the jaw and neck line. Research mostly concerns swallowing therapy and neck muscle activity; the jawline use is based on anecdote.

wall-angels.text: Used in posture routines to improve shoulder and upper-back mobility for a straighter, more open stance. It is common in rehab and fitness; no appearance trials were found.

thoracic-extension-over-foam-roller.text: Users do this mobility drill to counter rounded posture and stiffness, aiming for a more upright look. It appears in posture routines; no trials of the drill itself were found.

hip-flexor-stretching-couch-stretch.text: The couch stretch is used in posture circles to loosen the hip flexors and counter anterior pelvic tilt for a flatter-looking stomach and better stance. It is popular, with no trials on that use.

glute-bridges-glute-activation.text: Glute bridges are used to strengthen the glutes and, in posture circles, to counter anterior pelvic tilt for a flatter lower-back line. They also build glute size. Evidence for the posture use is absent.

chain: Stretch hips, strengthen glutes and core
anterior-pelvic-tilt-correction.text: Proponents use this routine to reduce pelvic tilt, citing a flatter-looking stomach, better posture and in some accounts more apparent height. It is widely recommended online and is thinly referenced and untested for looks.

core-stability-plank-dead-bug.text: Planks and dead bugs are pitched for posture and pelvic tilt and to firm the midsection. Core-stability research shows modest benefit over general exercise; appearance outcomes are untested.

mcgill-big-3.text: This three-exercise core routine from spine biomechanist Stuart McGill is used for back-sparing trunk strength and, in posture circles, for better carriage. Its use for looks is untested.

lower-trap-serratus-work.text: Exercises for the lower trapezius and serratus anterior are used in posture routines to hold the shoulder blades in place for a more open upper body. The anatomy is well described; the appearance benefit is untested.

rib-flare-correction-diaphragm-breathing.text: Posture communities use diaphragm breathing and core drills to pull protruding lower ribs back for a cleaner torso line. Proponents link rib flare to weak core and breathing mechanics; direct trials on appearance are almost absent.

jefferson-curl.text: Popular in strength circles as a mobility exercise for the spine and hamstrings, sometimes tied to posture. It has barely been studied, with one small 2026 EMG study, and its appearance use is anecdotal.
